rewrites.blindOutOfScope: No legal gender recognition; thin trans-specific data.

Media report (Nov 2018): the second Trans Day of Remembrance vigil was held in this country (with a local ally and veteran trans advocates named); a trans activist's first-person account of visibility and danger in the country.
Media report (Apr 2019): sentencing in a violent attack on a trans activist — no jail time handed down; reported via an advocate and a legal network — an impunity outcome visitors should weigh.

Commentary (Aug 2020): trans residents are frequently fired or denied jobs for 'dressing wrong'; an employment-protection bill does not cover them, and the country's remote-work visa markets openness while the anti-gay law stands.

Media report (Aug 2022): the regional supreme court struck down anti-buggery laws — the ruling covering this country decriminalised consensual same-sex conduct.

International LGBT-rights organisation country overview (updated March 2026): consensual same-sex conduct legal throughout the country since 2022 — the high court struck down provisions of the person-offences act (buggery and indecent assault against men) as contrary to privacy and expression rights; legal gender recognition is not possible; LGBTI organisations may register.

Civil-society submission to an international human-rights process (2025): decriminalisation in 2022 after a civil-society court challenge; LGBTQ+ citizens included in the national gender equality policy 2022-2027 but 'lack of tangible steps by the national government'; discrimination in the workplace, education, accommodation and hate speech is still not illegal; LGBTQ+ people avoid law enforcement.

Country status page (fetched 2026-09-29): criminalisation of homosexuality rescinded in 2022; the penal code still contains no discrimination or harassment protections on sexual orientation or gender identity; same-sex unions are not recognised in any form (marriage or partnership), and same-sex households receive none of the rights afforded to opposite-sex married couples; gender identity recognition unavailable.

Tag archive (fetched 2026-09-29): a collection led by the pieces 'Courts are the key to expanding LGBTQ rights' and 'Lawsuits target 5 nations' anti-gay laws' — advocacy coverage of the region's court-driven anti-sodomy-law challenges; the site tracks many countries' anti-gay laws and reports no post-repeal discrimination statute for this country.

rewrites.blindSummary: This country demands real caution. The high court decriminalised same-sex relations in April 2024 (the fourth state/province in the region); the old law had allowed forced psychiatric commitment. No legal gender recognition; small community; no documented anti-trans violence pattern.
rewrites.blindTangential: The 2024 decriminalisation removed same-sex-conduct exposure for visitors travelling with partners.
blindSourceSummaries: Human-rights organisation dispatch (24 Apr 2024): the country's high court decriminalised same-sex conduct; the piece's headline call is for all nations in the region to repeal similar criminal laws.

Media report (23 Apr 2024): the high court struck down sections 14 and 16 of the sexual-offences act criminalising consensual same-sex activity as unconstitutional, on a case brought by a gay man living in the country; activists hailed 'a significant milestone in the ongoing struggle for LGBTQ rights in the region'.
Source note: this is a national government press statement page (archived, navigation only at fetch time); the underlying statement relates to this country.

Diplomatic mission statement (22 Mar 2011): a statement on an international human-rights council's joint declaration 'ending acts of violence and related human rights violations based on sexual orientation and gender identity', signed by 85 countries — the signatory list explicitly includes this country, a dated diplomatic commitment on the record.

Local news outlet (20 Jul 2019): report of a high court challenge to the buggery and sexual-activity laws filed by the founder of a local rights organisation, announced at a news conference — contemporaneous evidence that the criminal provisions were under constitutional challenge five years before decriminalisation.

Media report (24 May 2013): a local Catholic bishop publicly called for eliminating criminal penalties for homosexuality and 'all forms of violence' against LGBT people, citing a global religious authority's position — documented local religious-authority stance against criminalisation.

News agency report: a court ruling that criminalising gay sex is unconstitutional — the regional litigation striking down the historic-era law (page largely navigation content at fetch time).

rewrites.blindSummary: This country demands real caution — the region's outlier: its high court UPHELD the buggery laws in 2024 (unlike its neighbours), so criminalisation (10 years) remains formally in force. Enforcement is rare, but the legal floor and judicial hostility distinguish it from the decriminalised neighbours.
rewrites.blindTangential: The buggery laws (10 years, upheld 2024) remain a formal exposure for visitors travelling with partners.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope: 2024 ruling upheld criminalisation — opposite trajectory from neighbours.
blindSourceSummaries: Source note: not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying human-rights organisation page documents regional constitutional challenges; this country retains historic-era buggery and gross-indecency laws.

Country profile: consensual homosexual acts between adults in private remain criminal under the inherited historic-era buggery act; many gay men marry women and live 'down-low'; social infrastructure is thin, with HIV-prevention groups the main contact point for MSM — an undated snapshot of social climate and legal shadow.

Media report (17 Feb 2024): the high court ruled on 16 Feb 2024 to uphold the ban on gay sex (provisions of the criminal code), dismissing a constitutional challenge — same-sex conduct stays criminal in this country.

Human-rights organisation (20 Jul 2023), 58-page report: LGBT people in this country face bias-motivated violence and discrimination in daily life; the organisation calls for decriminalising gay sex and passing SOGI non-discrimination legislation — core rights documentation for the country.

Regional rights alliance press release (19 Feb 2024): the alliance condemns the 16 Feb 2024 high court ruling upholding the same-sex conduct ban, saying LGBTQ+ residents face greater vulnerability — regional civil-society reaction with dated ruling outcome.

rewrites.blindSummary: This country demands real caution. The court of appeal struck down the sodomy law in 2016 — the region's first decriminalisation ruling; the country has an organised community and anti-discrimination employment protection. No legal gender recognition; gang violence in the main city is a general risk.
rewrites.blindTangential: The 2016 decriminalisation removed same-sex-conduct exposure for visitors travelling with partners.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope: No legal gender recognition; main-city violence is general.
blindSourceSummaries: Source note: not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying human-rights organisation page documents constitutional challenges to laws criminalising same-sex activity across the region, including this country (the 2016 ruling decriminalised same-sex conduct here).

International human-rights review coverage (2018): this country accepted 15 of 17 SOGI recommendations — the first country in the region to accept that many — pledging legal reform, explicit anti-discrimination legislation, police training and SOGI data collection; two rights-equality recommendations 'noted' rather than accepted.

National supreme court ruling (10 Aug 2016): the historic-era sodomy law provision was struck down as unconstitutional — the challenge a local LGBT advocate filed in 2010; landmark decriminalisation for the country.

Expat overview (2019): after the 2016 ruling — the first in the region to overturn its anti-sodomy law — gay travellers have long found this country friendly, though the rarely-enforced law had fostered intolerance (a 1998 protest showed residual hostility).

Live coverage (2013) of the constitutional challenge to the sodomy-law provision: the case tested in the main city, with day-by-day courtroom dispatches — the litigation that eventually produced the 2016 strike-down.
